# Verification, Feedback, and Learning {#sec-feedback-verification-trust}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence!"*
>
> — Edsger W. Dijkstra, *Notes on Structured Programming* (1970) [@Dijkstra1970Notes]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note.** Dijkstra's warning separates an architectural check from the broader claims we might attach to it. Passing testbenches only validates the specific conditions and workloads we exercised. A single failed assertion can decisively shatter a bounded claim about our design's correctness.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
When we receive signals from our AI-assisted design workflows, what do they actually tell us about our chosen actions, hardware artifacts, assumptions, or performance results? More importantly, how should we adapt our architectural strategies based on that feedback?
:::

A returned signal never explains itself. Verification performs the critical work of determining whether a given return is trustworthy and what architectural decisions it can legitimately support. In traditional workflows, human architects manually authored register-transfer level (RTL) code, ran static electronic design automation (EDA) verification passes at backend milestone gates, and evaluated single design points. In the Foundations of AI-Native Computing Systems, autonomous AI generators produce thousands of candidate hardware blocks in minutes, fast surrogate models predict power-performance-area (PPA) metrics continuously, and optimization loops search high-dimensional design spaces. This architectural evolution dramatically accelerates candidate synthesis, but it creates a massive verification bottleneck. While candidate generation scales exponentially, the property-specific qualification required to trust each candidate remains strictly governed by physical measurement and mathematical proof.

We use empirical checks to qualify the observed quantities we gather from benchmark runs, experiments, FPGA prototypes, or production systems. When we perform dynamic verification, we use targeted tests, cycle-accurate simulation, or hardware emulation to exercise our design and observe its specific behaviors. Formal methods allow us to use mathematical models and logic to establish the rigorous status of a property over a model under clearly stated assumptions [@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. We must treat these approaches as complementary rather than interchangeable.

Feedback is how we interpret these qualified results for a specific design component and identify our next justified engineering action. Learning then captures what our team improves or retains based on that interpretation. A given return might report a performance measurement, expose a deep pipeline failure, localize a critical path bottleneck, challenge a microarchitectural rationale, or leave a design question unresolved. Ultimately, we can only justify a recorded update to our designs when we explicitly document what tool produced the return, which hardware component it refers to, when it was obtained, and exactly what kind of architectural pivot it supports.

Our architectural studies inherently combine a massive variety of inputs. These include empirical measurements, formal verification bounds, trace-driven simulations, physical layout analysis, predictive model scores, peer design reviews, and real-world operational observations. We cannot assume these heterogeneous signals share a universal definition of a pass, a uniform type of uncertainty, or a single scope. As architects, we must qualify every return against the precise hardware property it attempts to address. We have to meticulously compare matched cases, explicitly expose the corner cases that remain unchecked, and actively route our results into the design process rather than passively letting the signal dictate its own application.

Today, our AI generators rapidly synthesize hardware candidates, our predictors score them instantly, and our optimizers search vast design spaces directly against imperfect power or area proxies. We also know that generated LLM explanations frequently express a degree of certainty that our empirical measurements cannot justify. This profound acceleration in our workflows does not absolve us of our strict, property-specific verification obligations. Every single generated candidate demands a rigorous check against a declared architectural property, an adequate golden reference model or expected-result rule, explicitly recorded environmental conditions, and comprehensive test coverage.

Furthermore, when we use AI to generate our tests or assertions, we immediately create new questions about the adequacy of those very checks. We find that while our capacity for candidate production can scale exponentially, the human-in-the-loop work required to rigorously qualify a result remains our fundamental bottleneck. AI fundamentally accelerates our process, but it does not change the high standard of what a valid computer architecture result must contain.

As the fourth technical building block of Architecture 2.0, verification and feedback transform raw tool execution into qualified evidence. Bringing our state representations (@sec-data-representations-world-models), search methods (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization), tool environments (@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces), and feedback mechanisms (@sec-feedback-verification-trust) together completes the technical building blocks of Architecture 2.0. This unified substrate enables us to transition from foundational technical building blocks to the active closed-loop execution and human architect ownership explored in Part III.



::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, we will be able to:

- Qualify tool returns by type and status to preserve data lineage.
- Construct matched architectural comparisons to isolate design impact.
- Interpret formal bounds and empirical uncertainty without overextending claims.
- Validate fast proxy metrics against bias, confounding, and selection risks.
- Apply qualified feedback to guide actions without treating every return as ML training data.
:::

## Qualified Architectural Actions and Decisions {#sec-from-feedback-to-decision}

To satisfy the high standards of a valid architectural result, we must first transform raw simulation traces and tool logs into qualified engineering evidence. An execution log records what ran, but it cannot tell us what a measurement actually means for our hardware design. While our design environment logs whether an execution attempt succeeded, failed, or timed out (@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces), converting those raw execution traces into sound design choices requires us to bridge the gap between tool output and architectural reasoning. Before we allow a returned metric to steer our pipeline parameters or microarchitectural choices, we must determine whether that signal genuinely reflects the physical property we intend to evaluate. From there, we establish what bounded claim our qualified result can support and which technical decisions we are ready to make.

Translating raw tool feedback into legitimate architectural revisions requires building a rigorous sequence of qualified claims before committing to design changes. First, we qualify the result to establish exactly what it means. Once we have that qualified result, we can use it to support a strictly bounded claim about our design. Only then does a specific architectural action become eligible, allowing us to safely lock in a design change or a learned lesson. We cannot skip steps here since a flaw early in this sequence invalidates all subsequent steps.

We should also remember that not every tool returns a hard measurement. We might receive a design review rationale, a model critique, a formal proof status from Cadence JasperGold, an enterprise formal property verification environment, a counterexample trace, or even a compiler warning. These qualitative outputs are highly valuable to our design process provided we carefully record their source, target, scope, timing, and inherent limitations. Whenever we get a raw numerical return, we must rigorously qualify it before we can trust it enough to compare different microarchitectural choices.

We have all seen tool setups fail, but we must recognize that a failed setup gives us absolutely no measurement at all. Even if our EDA process exits cleanly, it might still hand us a partial timing report from Cadence Tempus, an enterprise static timing analysis signoff tool, omit an essential power metric, report energy in the wrong units, or mistakenly parse an unfamiliar warning as a success. Conversely, a perfectly complete return might accurately report a genuine design rule or timing violation. Given these nuances, we must always preserve the raw execution status intact so our interpretation phase can accurately distinguish between a tool failure and an architectural failure.

When an evaluation run does not finish, we do not necessarily need to discard every artifact it generated, but we must tie any salvage operation to a specific architectural claim. We can only push an individual metric or artifact forward into qualification if our run specifications treat it as independently complete. Its extraction and lineage must be flawless, we must be certain that the premature termination did not alter its meaning or observation window, and our architectural claim cannot depend on any state that went missing. If any of these conditions fail, we must quarantine that artifact along with the failed run. Furthermore, successfully salvaging a single data point does not make our timed-out or incomplete attempt complete. Every other claim we hoped to evaluate remains strictly unresolved.

As architects reviewing these results, we must carefully separate five distinct questions. First, did our requested simulation or synthesis run actually execute? Second, is the artifact we got back structurally and semantically valid for the next step in our toolchain? Third, is the measurement or formal verification result valid under the conditions we stated? Fourth, which specific design requirement does this result satisfy or contradict, and what parts of our architecture remain untested? Finally, what concrete architectural conclusion or revision can we confidently support? Earning a "yes" to any one of these questions never automatically guarantees a "yes" to the ones that follow.

Consider what happens when we evaluate a 64-bit RISC-V compute subsystem (RV64GCV) featuring a vector-capable CPU, an NPU tensor matrix accelerator, and multi-die chiplet interconnects including Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) for high-bandwidth die-to-die streaming and Compute Express Link (CXL) for memory-coherent accelerator expansion. Our Lighthouse prompt stack anchors this subsystem against an XRBench real-time mobile XR workload alongside the SPEC CPU2026 CPU benchmark suite and MLPerf Mobile inference benchmark kernels under a 3\ W TDP target in a TSMC N7 or 3\ nm-class LP mobile process. As we lower software kernels from domain-specific JIT compilers through compiler Intermediate Representations (IRs like MLIR and LLVM IR) down to RISC-V Vector (RVV 1.0) assembly, we model internal Control-Data Flow Graphs (CDFGs) and memory traffic using systolic array traffic simulators and cycle-accurate DRAM timing simulators.[^fn-lighthouse-toolchain-c07]

When we synthesize an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) or generate an RTL block for this compute substrate using Yosys, an open-source RTL synthesis framework, or OpenROAD, an open-source digital physical design flow, the generation step might complete successfully and hand us the gate-level netlist, log files, and a preliminary timing report from OpenSTA, an open-source gate-level static timing analyzer. Even if that RTL parses cleanly, it might fail elaboration in Verilator, an open-source Verilog simulator, struggle with TSMC library binding, fail SystemVerilog Assertion (SVA) elaboration in Cadence JasperGold, an enterprise formal property verification environment, fail Bounded Model Checking (BMC) depth bounds, or fail an IEEE 1801 Unified Power Format (UPF) power-domain boundary check. If that happens, the artifact is functionally invalid for the rest of our tool path. Even if the design elaborates, static timing signoff tools like Cadence Tempus, an enterprise static timing analysis signoff tool, or thermal signoff tools like Ansys RedHawk-SC, a multiphysics power-grid and thermal signoff analyzer, might leave critical endpoints unconstrained or evaluate the wrong process corner, rendering the data entirely invalid for our physical claims. A qualified timing result only proves we met setup timing; our 3\ W TDP power envelope, UCIe/CXL interface protocol compliance, UPF power domain isolation, and formal SVA correctness remain uncovered, meaning we can never select our final architecture based on timing alone.

[^fn-lighthouse-toolchain-c07]: **Representative evaluation toolchain**: Our specific evaluation stack uses Triton for JIT compilation, SCALE-Sim, a cycle-accurate systolic array memory traffic simulator, for SRAM traffic simulation, Ramulator, a cycle-accurate DRAM timing simulator, for DRAM timing, Yosys, an open-source RTL synthesis framework, for synthesis, OpenROAD, an open-source digital physical design flow, for place and route, OpenSTA, an open-source gate-level static timing analyzer, and Verilator, an open-source Verilog simulator, for RTL simulation, Cadence JasperGold, an enterprise formal property verification environment, for formal property verification, Cadence Tempus, an enterprise static timing analysis signoff tool, for static timing signoff, and Ansys RedHawk-SC, a multiphysics power-grid and thermal signoff analyzer, for thermal signoff.

In @fig-evidence-flow, we trace how a raw tool return gains architectural meaning through a five-stage qualification pipeline: initial execution recording, result qualification, property-appropriate verification checks, feedback scoping, and final architectural learning. Our execution record first captures raw returns alongside their complete invocation lineage. Next, result qualification binds the metric type, target design object, semantic meaning, and operating corners. When supporting comparative claims, we introduce a matched comparator, while formal and physical returns pass through specialized verification checks (such as SystemVerilog Assertion bounds or static timing signoff). Scoping our feedback then defines precisely what the result supports and rules out unverified inferences before we update our design state or retain lessons. Crucially, the side routes in this process govern our iterative workflow. If we encounter an incomplete or corrupted return, we route it directly to execution repair to fix our tool environment. If a candidate fails an invalid comparison or property check, we loop back to reformulate our architectural study rather than prematurely discarding the design.

![**Tool returns gain architectural meaning through claim-specific result qualification.** Our execution record first supplies a return with its status and lineage. Our result qualification then binds its type, target, meaning, and operating conditions. When we make a comparison to support a comparative claim, we add a matched comparator. Our formal and other returns follow the property check appropriate to their type. Finally, our feedback step scopes our interpretation of exactly what the result supports and does not support before we record what to improve or retain in our architecture.](images/fig-evidence-flow){#fig-evidence-flow width="88%" fig-alt="A five-step flow from tool return through verification and a comparison or property check to feedback and a learning step that records what to improve or retain. Side paths send incomplete returns to execution repair and invalid checks to study formulation."}

Our checks establish the absolute limits of what a result can tell us. The feedback we gather does not automatically prescribe its own architectural update. Figuring out which specific design object needs our attention depends entirely on what produced the return, because our various simulation, synthesis, and formal verification tools expose fundamentally different properties, capabilities, and limitations.

## Evaluation Signal Sources and Feedback

Because no single verification tool or simulation framework can give us a complete picture of a complex system-on-chip, modern hardware evaluation forces us to synthesize a broad spectrum of heterogeneous signals, ranging from early human code reviews and fast analytical roofline models to multi-day gate-level timing runs and post-silicon telemetry. Because every evaluation source operates at a distinct spatial and temporal resolution, each carries its own inherent blind spots and abstraction errors.

To navigate these trade-offs, in @tbl-feedback-sources we systematically categorize our evaluation sources across four key columns: the Signal source itself, its Common form, its Timing and locality, and the Main quality question we must answer before using it. Our human reviewers contribute context-rich qualitative critiques and priority judgments, but their feedback is intermittent and requires explicit authority verification. Fast architecture tools and learned surrogate models offer immediate to high-density predictions, yet their observations remain strictly bounded by their underlying modeling assumptions and coverage. Hardware emulators (such as Siemens Veloce or Cadence Palladium) bridge this gap by providing multi-billion cycle full-system visibility at megahertz clock rates, though we must carefully qualify their transactor adapters and timing fidelity. Low-power static verifiers inspect UPF power state tables and isolation cells in minutes to hours, while physical signoff tools (such as Ansys RedHawk-SC or Cadence Tempus) and post-silicon telemetry deliver authoritative physical ground truth at the cost of high latency, high expense, and sparse component locality. Navigating these trade-offs requires us to downstream-qualify every signal against the specific hardware property it measures rather than treating any single tool as an infallible oracle.

| Signal source | Common form | Timing and locality | Main quality question |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Human reviewer | Critique, rationale, missing constraint, or priority judgment. | Intermittent and often context-rich. Locality depends on the review. | Does the reviewer have the relevant context, expertise, and authority, and is the rationale recorded? |
| Architecture tool or experiment | Scalar, trace, report, SVA counterexample, Cadence JasperGold proof status, gem5/Verilator coverage, or Tempus/RedHawk physical report. | Immediate to multi-day. May identify one path or only a terminal outcome. | Which property did the tool observe, under which conditions, with what coverage and error? |
| Hardware emulator | Multi-billion cycle full-system execution trace, OS boot log, or co-emulation profile from Siemens Veloce, Cadence Palladium, or Synopsys ZeBu hardware emulators. | High-speed (kHz to MHz). Provides full-system execution visibility before silicon tape-out. | Which speed adapters or transactors were applied, and does the target FPGA or emulator array accurately reflect chip-level timing? |
| Low-power verifier | Power state table (PST) violation, isolation cell leak, retention save/restore error, or static IEEE 1801 (UPF) rule report. | Fast static checks to multi-hour power-aware simulation runs. | Does the UPF specification accurately map to RTL power domains, level shifters, and power gating switches? |
| Learned model or method | Prediction, ranking, score, critique, or explanation. | Usually fast and dense. Often tied to the supplied representation. | Does the predicted score agree with stronger checks in the region being used, and which assumptions does it share with the producer? |
| Deployed system or silicon | Telemetry, characterization result, incident, or user-visible symptom. | Delayed and sparse. Often system-level rather than component-local. | Which population, version, workload, and unobserved causes limit the inference? |
: **Returned signals differ in form, timing, and locality.** We must determine whether a given signal is fit for the architectural learning or revision we expect it to support. {#tbl-feedback-sources tbl-colwidths="[16,23,29,32]"}

As architects, we should carefully select and qualify a source based on the specific property we are evaluating and the action we plan to take. We cannot simply treat the speed, density, or directness of an observation as a proxy for its evidentiary quality.

A delayed signal often reveals a final outcome without instructing us on how to remediate the underlying design. For instance, a grueling three-day physical signoff run using Ansys RedHawk-SC or Cadence Tempus might clearly show that our candidate violated IR-drop limits or missed setup timing under thermal stress. That terminal result does not tell us which of our thousands of microarchitectural or synthesis choices actually caused the violation. When dynamic thermal management (DTM) or IR-drop induced voltage droop causes cycle-stretching on CPU cores or NPU matrix engines, the raw signoff report only records a degraded wall-clock result. To meaningfully revise our design, we need signals at the right locality, such as path slack explicitly linked to the exact Control-Data Flow Graph (CDFG) node, Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) construct, compiler IR transformation, or netlist primitive that we just changed. Treating Ansys RedHawk-SC thermal and IR-drop feedback as a foundational constraint requires us to view it not merely as a backend signoff step, but as a core requirement that must actively inform our upstream microarchitectural choices and layout synthesis strategies from initial design formulation.

We can draw a useful precedent from feedback engineering, which distinguishes whether the state required for a corrective action is actually observable from the design of the action itself, while treating delay as an inherent part of the feedback path [@AstromMurray2008FeedbackSystems]. In our context, a multi-day simulation or synthesis run can leave the root cause of a failure only partially observable, even when the final chip-level outcome is clear. While we do not model architectural design search as a simple linear controller, we extract an essential lesson. The availability and latency of our signals strictly dictate which design corrections we can justify.

When handling these delayed results, we must start with strict lineage tracking rather than jumping straight to causal attribution. We need to bind every returned signal to our exact design candidate, parent actions, represented state, timing constraints, EDA tool versions, random seeds, simulation checkpoints, and the specific workloads that produced it. Provided our execution, setup, extraction, and checking conditions remain valid, a terminal result firmly establishes that our candidate missed timing under those exact parameters. It still does not tell us which earlier architectural decision caused the miss.

Our next step is to perform a distinguishing comparison. We must systematically analyze path endpoints, constraint coverage, routing congestion, power-density maps, and the structural differences between our current candidate and its parent or a matched sibling. If we uncover a stale constraint or a broken simulation setup, we route our revisions back to the environment or representation. If we see repeated failures across a matched class of design proposals, after verifying our shared setups, we can justify reopening our methodology to ask whether our representation, constraints, or proposal generation process needs an overhaul. Only when our comparison isolates a localized mechanism can we confidently justify a specific RTL or architectural revision. If our diagnostics cannot separate these possibilities, we should preserve the terminal outcome and leave the mechanism unresolved rather than arbitrarily assigning a negative label on every upstream action.

Deployment feedback follows this same principle. A production incident attaches first to the shipped silicon, system software, customer workload, and the specific operating conditions present at the time. While those extreme deployment conditions might reopen an earlier architectural claim, the production symptom itself does not identify the responsible design choice until we can support that attribution with an additional, targeted diagnostic or comparison.

Dense and immediate feedback is much easier for our methodologies to learn from, but we must remember that it is often just a proxy. The signals that observe our most decision-relevant properties, like silicon-accurate power or full-system performance under thermal constraints, are inevitably slower, vastly more expensive, and far less frequent. We can use fast proxy signals to guide our design search only within their rigorously qualified range, while relying on slower, less frequent sign-off checks to test the properties our proxies omit. Consequently, we must carefully qualify every signal in our workflow by its latency, spatial granularity, execution cost, inherent uncertainty, and the time required for interpretation and review.

We quantify this multi-stage physical verification bottleneck in @fig-synthesis-verification-funnel. In a benchmark study tracing 100,000 candidate proposals generated by language models across five sequential physical signoff stages, cumulative physical yield drops to $0.09\%$ by final layout signoff (only 91 candidates survive all five stages). Stage 1 ($72.4\%$ AST parse rate) screens syntactic errors; Stage 2 ($38.1\%$ pass rate) enforces AXI/TLM interface schema compliance; Stage 3 ($14.6\%$ pass rate) verifies functional SystemVerilog assertions in simulation; Stage 4 ($3.8\%$ pass rate) enforces static timing closure ($\text{WNS} \ge 0\text{ns}$); and Stage 5 ($59.5\%$ stage pass / $0.09\%$ final yield) achieves zero-DRC physical layout placement and routing closure [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM; @WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet; @WangEtAl2026AgentDSE; @ZhangEtAl2022AutoDSE].

![**Hardware synthesis and physical verification signoff funnel.** Panel A tracks candidate attrition across five signoff stages from 100,000 initial proposals down to 91 physically verified candidates ($0.09\%$ cumulative yield on secondary y-axis). Panel B plots stage-specific conditional pass rates given survival of prior stages [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM; @WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet; @WangEtAl2026AgentDSE; @ZhangEtAl2022AutoDSE].](images/fig-synthesis-verification-funnel.svg){#fig-synthesis-verification-funnel width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel visualization showing candidate attrition across five physical verification signoff stages from 100,000 proposals down to 91 surviving candidates (0.09% yield) alongside stage-specific conditional pass rates."}


## Empirical Admission Criteria

To determine whether a measured numerical value is eligible to enter architectural comparisons, we must establish strict empirical admission criteria. Empirical measurements form the backbone of architectural evaluation, yet every value extracted from simulation, synthesis, or hardware prototyping comes with inherent noise. Whether we collect cycle counts from gem5, a cycle-accurate architectural simulator, or timing slack from Verilator, an open-source Verilog simulator, our raw data carries sampling variation, numerical tolerances, and underlying model errors. We must strictly separate these practical empirical limits from the absolute logical bounds of formal mathematical proofs.

In @tbl-measurement-record, we outline the six required provenance record elements that explicitly bind candidate identity, metric units, operating conditions, extraction status, and error bounds before data enters decision-making.

To enforce this standard, our qualification workflow audits raw tool returns against six required record elements: Candidate identity, Quantity and unit, Conditions, Extraction status, Variation and error, and Source record. Candidate identity anchors the exact design revision and workload state under evaluation, while quantity and unit lock in the specific architectural metric and its aggregation rules. Operating conditions document the exact simulator version, process corners, and random seeds that produced the run. Extraction status verifies that the output log parsed cleanly under our schema without swallowing unfamiliar warnings. Variation and error capture trace sampling tolerances and known model boundaries, and source record maintains complete lineage back to the raw execution attempt.

| **Record Element** | **Question the record must answer** |
| --- | --- |
| Candidate identity | Which design revision, hardware configuration, software state, and workload produced the value? |
| Quantity and unit | What architectural metric was measured or computed, how did we aggregate it, and in what unit? |
| Conditions | Which simulation tool, power/timing model, corner, RNG seed, and operating conditions apply to this run? |
| Extraction status | Did the expected output artifact exist, parse successfully under our declared schema, and retain unfamiliar warnings? |
| Variation and error | What repetitions, trace sampling method, numerical tolerance, modeling error, or known bound restricts the value? |
| Source record | Which returned artifact and execution attempt support this metric, and can we fully recover the value from them? |
: **A measurement needs identity, meaning, conditions, and limits.** These record elements test whether our execution trace provides sufficient evidence for the architectural comparison we intend to make. {#tbl-measurement-record tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

We only allow a returned value to enter our design comparisons when these six elements make the data interpretable, establish its boundaries, and guarantee its recoverability from the original execution attempt. We treat these requirements together as a strict admission test rather than a set of independent quality scores. Passing this test does not automatically validate our architectural comparison. It simply qualifies the measured value as eligible to participate in one.

When we analyze sampled workloads across heterogeneous accelerators and CPU cores, our execution record must explicitly specify the unit of observation, the target instruction population, the trace sampling window, our aggregation method, and any dependence structure. Measuring instructions per cycle (IPC) in isolation without logging wall-clock execution time, thermal throttling states, or memory bus stall cycles fails to capture the true workload performance. When we track these parameters, we separate a merely mathematically correct computation from a robust estimate that authentically represents the workload population and drives valid architectural decisions.

Our simulation and synthesis environments provide the raw returned artifacts, extraction statuses, recorded operating conditions, and precise data lineage. We cannot rely on measurement qualification to synthetically reconstruct missing RTL versions or retroactively rerun a log parser. Qualification asks whether our specified quantity, aggregation strategy, error margins, chosen comparator, and checking scope render the extracted metric genuinely usable for architectural evaluation. If we find missing execution parameters, we must repair our experimental environment. Conversely, if we uncover inadequate trace observations or fundamentally flawed design comparisons, we must overhaul the study itself.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="A returned value must qualify before it becomes feedback"}
**Context.** Imagine we are evaluating a prospective larger L2 cache configuration for an RV64GCV vector-capable CPU and NPU accelerator block running an XRBench real-time mobile XR workload alongside SPEC CPU2026 and MLPerf Mobile benchmark traces. The software pipeline lowers Triton JIT blocks into RVV 1.0 vector primitives, with data movement modeled using SCALE-Sim SRAM buffers and Ramulator LPDDR5X DRAM timing under a 3\ W TDP envelope in a 3\ nm-class LP mobile process (TSMC N7). During verification, static IEEE 1801 (UPF) power-domain checks pass, but a Bounded Model Checking (BMC) run in Cadence JasperGold or an SVA property check ends in a stale-state setup failure, while an Ansys RedHawk-SC thermal signoff summary report omits raw trace lineage. Neither scenario constitutes retained execution evidence.

**Required record.** For rigorous qualification across all 8 layers of our prompt stack, we need the exact workload trace (XRBench, SPEC CPU2026, MLPerf), ISA contract (RV64GCV), compute organization, memory simulation models (SCALE-Sim, Ramulator), power envelope (3\ W TDP), compiler lowering state (Triton JIT to RVV 1.0), physical process conditions (TSMC N7 / 3\ nm-class LP), and verification artifacts (UPF IEEE 1801, SVA, BMC, RedHawk-SC). We also require the terminal status, raw return data, extraction status, units, operating conditions, and specific bounds.

**Action.** We must route the stale-state failure back for environment repair while retaining its recorded failure class. We keep the subsequent unverified thermal value strictly unqualified until we can supply its missing record. We do not reject any architectural candidate based on either flawed case.

**Takeaway.** Mere chronological progress does not transform an infrastructure failure or an unrecoverable data summary into valid architectural design evidence.
:::

Until our execution records fully qualify, we cannot support any claims about a design candidate's outcome or its underlying architectural mechanisms. Once we qualify a measurement, it safely enters the rigorous comparisons demanded by our core architecture questions. Qualification establishes the precise meaning of a single returned value, whereas comparison reveals the true architectural differences between our proposed candidate and a declared baseline alternative under carefully matched conditions.

We must also remember that empirical uncertainty and formal proof status answer fundamentally different questions. An empirical confidence interval summarizes hardware variation under a specific sampling and repetition procedure. How we interpret it depends heavily on the target instruction population, our chosen statistic, dependence structures, modeling errors, and required decision margins. In contrast, a formal verification result is never just a narrow empirical interval. It carries absolutely no sampling confidence level. It reports a definitive logical outcome for a mathematically stated property, machine model, and set of assumptions. While solver timeouts in Cadence JasperGold, proof depth boundaries, and memory constraints might limit a formal proof's scope or completion, they never degrade its statistical confidence. Before we resume any architectural comparison, our formal returns demand their own parallel qualification path that strictly evaluates the stated property, the formal model, the underlying assumptions, and the ultimate proof scope.

## Formal Proof Bounds and Equivalence

Unlike empirical simulations that sample execution space, formal verification yields exact mathematical bounds over specified property, model, and assumption tuples. This mathematical rigor demands a dedicated qualification path. Because a formal proof holds only within its stated boundary conditions, we must carefully evaluate how formal proof statuses, bounded search limits, and sequential equivalence mappings translate into physical hardware guarantees.

### Proof Statuses and Traces

Formal verification shares our primary qualification path, yet it operates without requiring a matched comparator design. Instead, a formal status relies on a tight triad consisting of the property, the model, and the governing assumptions. First, our property explicitly states the architectural behavior we need to verify, typically written as SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA). Anchoring SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) as core microarchitectural contracts means treating them not as optional testbench aids, but as mathematically binding statements that define the core correctness of our microarchitecture. Second, our model precisely defines the state, transitions, and specific artifacts over which we interpret that property. Finally, our assumptions carefully constrain the inputs, environmental behaviors, resets, clock domains, protocols, and neighboring components in formal tools like Cadence JasperGold or Synopsys VC Formal, a formal property verification environment. For our formal results to carry real meaning, we must carry all three elements together. If we construct a proof over an inaccurate model or force an impossible assumption, we might generate a logically sound result that is ultimately useless for our architectural goals.

We often find that the model we actually check differs from the raw RTL or implementation artifact outlined in our architecture claims. Processes like elaboration, extraction, and abstraction frequently add or discard specific behaviors to make the proof tractable in engines like Jasper. Consequently, our results must explicitly state the exact correspondence our verification flow preserves between the abstract model and the final artifact, justifying why this relationship successfully maps the proved property back to our silicon [@Clarke2018ModelChecking].

We must also trust our checking base, which comprises the sequence of steps and components that transform our architectural artifact and its requirements into the mathematical problem the solver evaluates. Our documentation must rigorously identify the elaboration or model extraction procedures, property translations, relevant SVA libraries and scripts, the specific solver or proof checker used, and any available certificate or replay path. We can easily produce a logically valid proof for a mistranslated property or an improperly extracted model, only to fail the underlying architecture requirement. Whenever our tooling yields a checkable proof certificate or replay artifact, we should diligently retain it. If a tool offers no such artifact, we must avoid implying that one exists in our records.

We must ensure our project records clearly distinguish whether the checker produced a complete proof, generated a counterexample trace, reached a bounded-only result, or simply remained inconclusive. Each distinct status dictates a very specific set of next actions for our engineering teams. We cannot simply relabel one result as another simply because we are under pressure to reach closure.

When examining counterexamples from formal engines, we need to make one critical distinction before we begin any repairs. In counterexample-guided abstraction refinement (CEGAR), we often encounter spurious counterexamples that exist solely because our abstract model permits behaviors inherently blocked by the concrete hardware [@ClarkeEtAl2000CEGAR]. These traces guide us in refining the abstraction itself, rather than proving our design is fundamentally flawed. If a trace in a DMA controller or NPU memory management unit survives our concretization process and setup reviews, it likely exposes a genuine architectural defect or an incorrectly specified requirement. We must treat CEGAR as a highly specific formal-verification procedure rather than a generic label for any feedback loop. Ultimately, the exact nature of the counterexample dictates whether we must repair our abstraction, rethink our hardware design, or rewrite our requirement.

### Bounded Search and Vacuity

Bounded Model Checking (BMC) provides an essential early diagnostic that searches for property violations within a finite state horizon [@BiereEtAl1999BMC]. Rather than viewing BMC as merely an incomplete proof, we treat it as a foundational diagnostic instrument that systematically eliminates shallow state-space errors before we attempt full inductive proofs. If we fail to find a counterexample within this limit, we still cannot definitively rule out a deeper failure later in execution. To claim unbounded safety, we must either provide a rigorous completeness argument or deploy an unbounded method like induction or property-directed reachability techniques such as IC3/PDR [@Bradley2011IC3; @EenEtAl2011PDR]. Even after achieving an unbounded proof, we must remember that our result only validates the specifically stated property across our modeled transition system and its localized assumptions.

We must carefully distinguish between safety and liveness claims in our architectures. A safety property strictly excludes negative behaviors, such as preventing two disparate requesters from simultaneously holding exclusive ownership of a single cache line or NPU tile buffer. Proving this safety property without bounds still tells us nothing about system progress. To guarantee progress, we use liveness properties, which mandate that an accepted request will eventually receive a proper response [@AlpernSchneider1985Liveness; @Clarke2018ModelChecking]. While a bounded check might expose a stalled execution or a localized deadlock within our search horizon, it cannot prove that our system remains free from starvation or permanent deadlock over infinite time. For any unbounded progress claim, we require a liveness-capable proof or a rigorously justified reduction. We must retain the specific fairness assumptions that preclude actions from being indefinitely postponed. If we adopt unrealistic fairness assumptions, we risk masking severe architectural progress defects. Therefore, our final results must transparently record the property class, our chosen fairness assumptions, the precise proof method, and any specific bounds or reductions we applied.

We must remain vigilant against properties passing without genuinely checking our intended behaviors. We encounter vacuity when the antecedent condition meant to trigger an SVA property never actually occurs during formal execution, making the logical implication vacuously true [@BeerEtAl2001Vacuity; @Clarke2018ModelChecking]. Even a nonvacuous property can be structurally weak. It might tolerate a response arriving thousands of cycles late, omit mutual exclusivity constraints, ignore reset sequencing entirely, or monitor one requester while leaving others unconstrained. To combat this, we exercise our properties using SVA cover statements, verifying reachable triggers, checking against known positive and negative cases, applying mutation testing, and constantly reviewing them against high-level architectural requirements. While modern frameworks like AssertLLM, an automated assertion generation framework, can automatically generate SystemVerilog assertions from design specifications and verify them against golden register-transfer-level (RTL) models using formal property verification [@FangEtAl2025AssertLLM], we remain vulnerable. If both our RTL and our generated assertions inherit the identical missing requirement, a clean proof tells us absolutely nothing about the omitted architectural behavior.

We must treat these generated assertions as critical verification artifacts that demand strict qualification in their own right. Recent studies of LLM assertion generation demonstrate that general-purpose models often produce substantial fractions of syntactically and semantically invalid assertions, although task-specific, fine-tuned models markedly improve performance across those two dimensions [@PulavarthiEtAl2025AssertionGeneration]. Regardless of their origin, we must rigorously verify their syntax and elaboration in formal tools or simulators, assess their semantic strength, confirm their coverage of our intended architectural properties, and evaluate whether they successfully trap intentionally seeded bugs or known historical defects. Although these robust checks make automated assertion generation significantly more useful in our design flows, they can never guarantee that our resulting property set is mathematically or architecturally complete.

### Equivalence and Refinement

Equivalence checking addresses a fundamental hardware design question regarding whether a transformed implementation faithfully preserves the structural or behavioral properties of a golden reference design. We often use combinational equivalence checking (CEC) to pair state elements as structural cut points, allowing us to easily compare the combinational logic sandwiched between them. We must escalate to sequential equivalence checking (SEC) whenever our architectural transformations, such as aggressive retiming in NPU vector pipelines, pipelined latency adjustments, insertion of additional state, or modifications to reset mappings, alter the direct correspondence across state or time boundaries. We must keep in mind that neither technique proves that our reference artifact actually embodies the intended architecture [@Kropf1999FormalVerification].

We also find that strict equivalence is often far too rigid, particularly when our RTL implementations intentionally introduce microarchitectural details or permit fewer non-deterministic behaviors than our high-level specifications. In these cases, we rely on a refinement check, asking instead whether every implementation behavior allowed by our mapping firmly respects the broader specification. Because we routinely decompose large proofs by component, we frequently rely on assume-guarantee reasoning. Under this framework, each individual block, such as an NPU matrix tile or a CPU load-store unit, proves its guarantee only as long as its surrounding environment satisfies a set of explicitly named assumptions. Our overall system composition remains sound only if the neighboring blocks' guarantees successfully discharge those assumptions [@BenvenisteEtAl2018Contracts]. We must never assume a localized block proof silently scales into a whole-system proof. Consequently, our refinement mappings, precise component boundaries, interface assumptions, and any unproved remainders must all be documented as integral parts of our final verification result.

### Formal Bounds Versus Dynamic Coverage

Rigorous architectural verification requires us to trace every core requirement directly to the specific formal property or dynamic test suite designed to evaluate it. Our documentation must transparently link the original requirement source and the claimed RTL back to the checked model, its governing SVA properties, bounding assumptions, and any applied abstraction or extraction relations. To extend finite Bounded Model Checking (BMC) depth $k$ into an unbounded safety proof, we use $k$-induction:

$$B(k) \wedge I(k) \implies P$$

where the base step $B(k) = \bigwedge_{i=0}^k P(s_i)$ verifies that property $P$ holds for all reachable states up to depth $k$, and the inductive step $I(k) = \left( \bigwedge_{i=0}^k P(s_i) \right) \implies P(s_{k+1})$ proves that any valid sequence of length $k$ preserves $P$ into state $k+1$. Furthermore, to defend against AI-generated over-constrained assumptions (a vacuous proof trap where an agent inserts contradictory `assume` statements $A \equiv \bot$ to force $A \implies P$ to pass trivially), we enforce a mandatory assumption satisfiability check:

$$\text{is\_sat}(A) = \text{true}$$

for every assumption $A \in s_{\text{env}}$ before accepting a formal proof status. Furthermore, we require explicit access to the proof method and its final status, the bound or completeness rationale in Cadence JasperGold, evidence defending against vacuity through cover traces, our chosen refinement or composition boundaries, and an explicit declaration of any unverified remaining logic. Even if we secure a pristine set of clean proofs, we must acknowledge that this does not inherently prove our property set is architecturally complete.

We approach dynamic simulation with a different set of claims. In our workflows, directed tests, constrained-random stimuli in Verilator or Synopsys VCS, an event-driven Verilog simulator, coverage-guided generation, large-scale hardware emulation, formal methods, and post-silicon testing all complement one another, primarily because exhaustive dynamic simulation remains completely infeasible for modern chips [@Kropf1999FormalVerification]. We use code coverage to report on the specific structural elements we managed to exercise during execution. Meanwhile, we apply functional coverage to track the specific architectural events or data bins defined in our verification plans. SystemVerilog standardizes functional-coverage constructs like covergroups, coverpoints, discrete bins, and crosses to help us quantify our progress [@IEEE2023SystemVerilog]. Yet, we must concede that neither coverage family can mathematically guarantee what fraction of the totally reachable behavior we actually checked. Conversely, our formal proofs can never verify a property we failed to write down.

To bridge the throughput gap between slow software RTL simulation and full silicon execution, we deploy enterprise hardware emulation platforms such as Siemens Veloce, Cadence Palladium, and Synopsys ZeBu. When we compile synthesizable RTL onto custom hardware processor arrays or dense FPGA fabrics, emulation accelerates execution speeds by 1,000x to 10,000x over event-driven software simulators. This massive speedup allows us to boot complete operating systems, execute multi-billion-cycle ML inference workloads, and evaluate complex hardware-software co-design decisions prior to tape-out. We use transaction-level transactors and speed adapters to interface virtual software models with high-speed emulator hardware, allowing software teams to validate production drivers and firmware against target register-transfer logic. Emulation delivers high throughput, but we must carefully account for its reduced signal visibility compared to software waveform traces and verify that clocking abstractions introduced during emulator compilation do not mask microarchitectural race conditions.

Modern energy-efficient architectures also demand explicit low-power verification to validate power gating, dynamic voltage scaling, and multi-rail power topologies. We specify low-power architectural intent through the IEEE 1801 Unified Power Format (UPF), a standardized specification language that decouples power domain intent from functional RTL logic. Within UPF, a power state table (PST) defines a formal state matrix governing the legal operating voltage combinations across interdependent power domains, ensuring that level shifters and isolation cells prevent floating signals or protocol violations during low-power transitions. Low-power verification requires us to combine static UPF rule checking with low-power aware (LPA) simulation and formal UPF verification. Static UPF checks verify that every signal path crossing power domain boundaries includes an appropriate isolation cell and level shifter. Low-power aware simulation explicitly models signal corruption during power-down, retention save and restore sequences, and voltage domain transitions. If a power state machine triggers an illegal power state transition or fails to isolate an active receiver from a powered-down driver, UPF verification flags the floating signal or protocol violation before logic synthesis and layout signoff.

When we examine the historic Pentium floating-point division (FDIV) failure, published accounts and Bob Colwell's The Pentium Chronicles detail both the underlying microarchitectural flaw and the staggering $475M pre-tax replacement charge Intel absorbed [@Edelman1997PentiumDivision; @Intel1995PentiumCharge; @Colwell2006PentiumChronicles].

::: {.callout-war-story title="The Pentium FDIV flaw and the limit of sampled testing"}
**The claim.** Pre-silicon execution-unit verification relied on constrained-random dynamic simulation, which passed millions of floating-point division vectors without discovering a flaw.

**The gap.** In the Radix-4 SRT division lookup table, 5 entries out of 1,066 in the Programmable Logic Array (PLA) were inadvertently omitted during script-driven array generation [@Edelman1997PentiumDivision; @Colwell2006PentiumChronicles]. Because the defect manifested in only 1 out of every 9 billion random division operations, dynamic simulation completely missed the missing PLA entries.

**The lesson.** Sampled dynamic simulation cannot mathematically guarantee the absence of rare corner-case defects in high-dimensional state spaces. In response, modern processor teams transformed formal property verification from a research experiment into an obligatory signoff gate for execution units [@KaivolaEtAl2009Corei7Formal].
:::


In the aftermath of such failures, we have seen formal verification evolve into the primary validation method for complex logic, such as the execution cluster within Intel's Core i7 design flow [@KaivolaEtAl2009Corei7Formal]. Having firmly established this parallel qualification path in our discipline, we map the four formal result statuses to highly distinct technical actions in our engineering workflows as detailed in @tbl-formal-result-status.

When we process formal verification returns from tools like Cadence JasperGold, our decision pipeline maps each of the four possible formal statuses (Proved, Counterexample, Bounded-only, and Inconclusive) directly to an eligible downstream action. A Proved status conclusively discharges an architectural claim within its strictly declared property bounds and assumptions. A Counterexample returns a concrete violating trace, triggering abstraction refinement when Counterexample-Guided Abstraction Refinement (CEGAR) identifies a spurious artifact, or driving RTL repair when the trace represents a real architectural bug. A Bounded-only result confirms no counterexamples exist up to a finite cycle depth, requiring us to record that limit without claiming unbounded safety. Finally, an Inconclusive outcome signals that the solver ran out of memory or time, obligating us to re-parameterize the proof budget or revise our abstractions rather than misreporting the run as a pass.

| **Formal status** | **What it establishes** | **Eligible next action** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Proved** | We have established that the declared property or equivalence holds for the recorded model and assumptions, conditional on our property translation, the model-to-artifact relationship, our trusted checking components, and an available certificate or replay path. Our proof method need not be complete for a proved result to be valid. | We record the strictly scoped result and discharge only the architectural claim explicitly covered by that property, model, assumptions, and proof mode. |
| **Counterexample** | We have found a modeled trace that violates the property. Our setup, assumptions, and concretization routines will dictate whether this trace represents a truly realizable architecture failure. | We refine our abstraction whenever CEGAR identifies a spurious trace. Otherwise, we repair the design or requirement contradicted by a fully reviewed, realizable trace. |
| **Bounded-only** | We found no counterexample through our declared simulation horizon. We establish absolutely nothing beyond that bound without a separate, rigorous completeness argument. | We record the finite bound and we either extend or change our checking method if the broader architectural claim matters, or we explicitly leave that claim open. |
| **Inconclusive** | Our solver supplied neither a proof nor a counterexample because it returned unknown, exhausted available compute resources, or simply failed to complete the proof procedure. | We systematically revise the abstraction, interface assumptions, proof method, or compute resource budget. We must never report this result as a pass. |
: **Formal result status dictates next technical actions in verification feedback.** A proof discharges only its carefully scoped claim, while counterexamples, finite bounds, and incomplete proofs force us to attempt different repairs or leave our broader architectural claims open. {#tbl-formal-result-status tbl-colwidths="[16,45,39]"}

## Matched Baseline and Candidate Comparisons {#sec-evidence-specific-to-claim-and-scope}

Once individual empirical measurements and formal proof bounds are qualified for admission, we can construct the comparative evaluations that guide design choices. Architectural decisions rarely turn on absolute performance metrics in isolation; they depend on relative differences between candidate designs. Determining whether a microarchitectural modification truly improves performance requires us to isolate genuine hardware gains from confounding experimental noise, construct valid paired differences under strictly matched workloads, and guard our search against statistical pitfalls such as the optimizer's curse.

If we are conducting a cache replacement study, we must ask how our candidate architecture behaves relative to a baseline under identical workloads and system software states. We can certainly compare two candidate designs generated by entirely different synthesis processes, but we must recognize that the result reflects only their measured architectural difference, not necessarily the overall quality of the methodologies that produced them. Therefore, we treat the comparator as an integral part of our design claim rather than a mere footnote appended after the fact.

Every comparison we make binds our specific candidate and comparator revisions to a single, measured difference, inextricably linking them to the precise conditions that constrain that measurement. In @fig-claim-frame, we structure our evidence across three connected blocks: design inputs on the left, measured outputs in the center, and strict boundary conditions surrounding them. Our candidate design revision and baseline comparator feed directly into a shared evaluation engine to compute a single, unified metric quantity and unit. The center block extracts the raw paired difference alongside its statistical uncertainty model (such as a confidence interval derived from block bootstrapping). Crucially, the outer frame establishes that this measured difference is non-transferable; it remains strictly bounded by the underlying software workload, initial microarchitectural state, EDA synthesis flags, process-voltage-temperature (PVT) corners, and the exact property observed by our verification check.

![**Comparative claim frames bind candidate and baseline designs to measured deltas.** We evaluate our candidate and comparator designs for the exact same quantity and unit. Our result inherently remains conditional on the specific workload, architectural state, synthesis tool constraints, uncertainty models, and the exact property our verification check can observe.](images/fig-claim-frame){#fig-claim-frame width="100%" fig-alt="Three-column comparison frame. Candidate and comparator feed a measured quantity, difference, and uncertainty, which are bounded by workload and design state, tool conditions, and check scope."}

If we change the workload, architectural state, EDA tool constraints, uncertainty model, or even the observable hardware property, we fundamentally create an entirely new comparison even if the center numerical value remains unchanged. When we rigorously maintain these bindings, we prevent ourselves from erroneously carrying a measured numerical difference over into operating conditions or architectural claims that we never actually evaluated.

For our set of matched architectural cases $c_j$, we define the fundamental paired difference as

$$
d_j = y(\text{candidate}, c_j) - y(\text{comparator}, c_j).
$$

We must explicitly state our sign convention. In our evaluations, a positive value might indicate a throughput improvement, yet simultaneously represent a severe latency regression. Whenever we report a percentage, we must clearly define its denominator. Similarly, when we present an aggregate metric, we must specify whether it represents a mean, a specific tail percentile, a maximum bound, a geometric mean, or some other statistical measure. When dealing with positive performance ratios normalized against a reference design, we rely on the geometric mean to preserve a consistent relative interpretation across an entire benchmark suite. If we were to use an arithmetic mean of those ratios, our conclusions could artificially swing depending on which architectural baseline we arbitrarily chose as the reference [@FlemingWallace1986HowNotToLie]. Unless we make and document these methodological choices clearly, we risk combining two mathematically correct numbers into a completely incoherent architectural comparison.

### Confounding Factors

Isolating a microarchitectural intervention requires that our candidate and baseline designs differ strictly in the specific hardware mechanisms under study. Factors such as the software workload, simulation model version in gem5 or ChampSim, a trace-driven memory hierarchy simulator, synthesis tool flags, voltage/frequency operating points, dynamic thermal management (DTM) states, cache warmup periods, trace sampling windows, and total resource budgets can easily introduce massive performance deltas that have absolutely nothing to do with our proposed hardware change. To build a truly matched comparison, we meticulously record all of these factors rather than sloppily relying on similar output filenames or shared project directories.

We often hope that systematic modeling errors will naturally cancel out in a relative comparison. This cancellation only occurs if our simulator or analytical model treats the candidate and comparator identically across the specific design space region we are studying. We can sometimes use a frozen, slightly inaccurate simulator to confidently establish a rank ordering of designs even if its absolute predictions diverge from post-silicon reality. This fragile bargain completely collapses if our proposed architecture change crosses an unmodeled microarchitectural boundary or triggers a pathological behavior in only one of the candidates. Ultimately, we must treat error cancellation as a rigorous hypothesis that we actively verify, rather than an automatic property we inherit simply through applying the same evaluation framework [@GutierrezEtAl2014SourcesOfError; @PeherstorferWillcoxGunzburger2018Multifidelity].

### Paired Differences

High variance in benchmark execution traces or stochastic synthesis runs makes single-point measurements inherently untrustworthy. When our tools or workloads exhibit substantial dispersion, we rely on repeated measurements to quantify run-to-run variance. We can use paired resampling techniques to preserve the critical relationship between our matched baseline and candidate execution frames.[^fn-paired-block-resampling-c07] The object we resample is the paired-difference sequence $d_j$, rather than treating the baseline and candidate as two independently resampled streams. The confidence interval we derive from this process inherently assumes that our sequence remains sufficiently stationary over the sampled execution region, and that our declared block length successfully captures the temporal dependence relevant to our chosen statistic. Because architectural evaluations face compounding variations from numerical tolerances, finite trace sampling, heuristic synthesis algorithms, and underlying model errors, we often require specialized statistical treatments for each. We cannot simply apply a single generic error bar to our graphs and expect it to represent all of these distinct sources of architectural uncertainty.

[^fn-paired-block-resampling-c07]: **Paired block resampling**: A block bootstrap resamples contiguous segments of our paired-difference sequence. When we enforce this pairing, we keep each matched baseline and candidate case tightly bound together, while the block structure preserves local temporal dependence according to the method's underlying assumptions [@Kunsch1989BlockBootstrap].

Let us consider a hypothetical, fully retained matched simulation run where we define improvement as our baseline latency minus our candidate latency. In this framing, a positive value indicates our candidate architecture is faster. Suppose our point estimate shows a 0.3\ ms speedup, but our 95 percent confidence interval stretches from -0.1\ ms to 0.7\ ms. Keep in mind these are invented teaching values, not empirical measurements drawn from a retained Lighthouse framework run. If our future evaluation properly retains the matched execution frame sequences and applies a rigorously declared paired block-resampling procedure, we would see that this interval spans both a minor performance regression and a much larger improvement. Because the interval crosses zero, this hypothetical comparison fundamentally leaves our architectural tail-latency question unresolved, regardless of how favorable the central point estimate might appear.

To strengthen our evaluations, we can introduce a decision margin as a secondary test. If our architectural study requires a minimum practical improvement of at least $m$, our comparison must resolve the final result relative to $m$, rather than merely checking if it is greater than zero. Whenever our measured difference falls inside the boundaries of known measurement resolution or statistical uncertainty, we must accept that the outcome remains unresolved. While we might appropriately label this scenario a tie under a strict, predeclared evaluation rule, we can never legitimately claim it as an architectural improvement.

### The Optimizer's Curse

A meticulously controlled experimental setup protects against confounding variables, but it cannot prevent us from misinterpreting statistical noise during automated exploration. Confounding effects emerge whenever an undocumented or unintended factor could equally account for our observed performance gains. To isolate our intended microarchitectural changes from other plausible alternatives, we must routinely employ stable tool versions, rigorous ablation studies, heavily controlled matched contrasts, and exhaustive sensitivity analyses.

Selection bias introduces yet another severe pitfall in our design methodologies. If our design space exploration evaluates thousands of noisy candidate architectures and we only report the single best performer, our selected peak value inherently retains some of the statistical luck that helped it win in the first place. Simply re-evaluating the same search data does absolutely nothing to remove this bias [@SmithWinkler2006OptimizersCurse]. To validate our findings, we must conduct a fresh evaluation that measures our chosen candidate architecture against entirely new random seeds, disjoint workloads, or operating cases that played no part in the initial selection phase. This secondary evaluation forces us to answer whether our performance margin actually persists across independent operating conditions, long after our automated search process has stopped selecting peak outcomes based on noisy measurements.

Finally, we must recognize that even our most carefully matched comparison might rely on an evaluation proxy that fails to translate into a realistic, post-silicon architectural result. Moreover, a highly favorable performance outcome does not automatically prove that our proposed hardware mechanism is actually functioning the way we think it is. Therefore, we must perform rigorous proxy qualification and dedicated mechanism testing as completely separate verification steps, to be executed only after we have successfully matched all candidate and comparator conditions.

## Qualifying Proxies and Calibration {#sec-proxy-mismatch-metric-gaming-and-calibration}

Even when baseline and candidate conditions are meticulously matched, accelerating high-dimensional architectural exploration forces us to rely on low-cost evaluation proxies. Yet a surrogate metric is useful only if its rankings faithfully reflect physical reality. When we rely on a cheaper signal, it must track our target architectural quantity closely enough to support the actual design decision we are making. We must detect and prevent microarchitectural proxy gaming, validate numerical calibration across held-out conditions, and strictly separate observed architectural outcomes from their underlying causal mechanisms. A qualified proxy is undeniably useful, but it cannot answer the mechanism question on its own.

### Proxy Metric Gaming

Fast evaluation surrogates enable us to screen millions of design points in seconds, but optimizing directly against an incomplete proxy introduces profound risks. Metrics like estimated instructions per cycle (IPC), analytical 0-cost memory roofline bounds, wirelength, routing congestion, hardware utilization, and simulated cycle counts all help us rank design candidates. We must remember they remain partial measurements. The danger rapidly grows when we point an automated optimizer directly at these proxies, driving what we term microarchitectural proxy gaming. This failure mode occurs when a search algorithm exploits mathematical approximations or unmodeled physical edge cases in a fast proxy metric (such as nominal IPC, simplified SRAM access latency, or 0-cost analytical fold bounds that assume 100 percent L1 cache hit ratios) to maximize the proxy score while severely degrading true physical performance (such as wall-clock execution time under severe DRAM bank-conflict serialization, total thermal design power, or IR-drop stability under dynamic thermal throttling).

We inadvertently reward our search algorithms for finding every corner of the design space where our proxy and our intended architectural result diverge. Elevating microarchitectural proxy gaming to a core principle demands that we treat metric exploitation not as an algorithmic bug, but as the inevitable and primary failure mode of any search methodology optimizing an incomplete representation of physical reality.

This phenomenon is Goodhart's problem manifesting in computer architecture. A measure that originally tracked a design goal can abruptly stop tracking it once we make it our primary optimization target [@Goodhart1975MonetaryManagement; @Strathern1997Goodhart]. While AI-driven design methodologies are not unique in exposing this behavior, they fundamentally change the scale and persistence with which they search for loopholes in our evaluation metrics. To prevent neural optimizers from exploiting these metric blind spots, we deploy neurosymbolic design methodologies that pair probabilistic neural candidate generation with symbolic verifiers and Satisfiability Modulo Theories solvers. When we embed formal SystemVerilog Assertion bounds directly into the neural search loop, we enforce exact mathematical constraints on the generator, bounding probabilistic errors before candidate architectures reach physical signoff tools.

Consider proxy gaming across an RV64GCV vector-capable CPU core and NPU matrix accelerator targeting XRBench, SPEC CPU2026, and MLPerf Mobile workloads. An optimizer directed at nominal IPC on an NPU systolic array might aggressively widen execution queues or introduce deep speculative pipelining. While nominal IPC on synthetic matrix multiplication kernels increases, the added logic breaches our 3\ W TDP target and raises peak power density in a TSMC N7 or 3\ nm-class LP mobile process. When lowered from Triton JIT to RVV 1.0 vector code, SCALE-Sim SRAM traffic and Ramulator DRAM bus models show increased memory latency. In physical signoff, thermal tools like Ansys RedHawk-SC or static timing analyzers like Cadence Tempus reveal that this power density triggers dynamic thermal management (DTM) throttling or severe IR-drop voltage droop. As a result, clock frequencies are scaled down or memory bus stall cycles multiply, causing wall-clock execution time to severely regress despite the deceptively high nominal IPC score. Similarly, on vector-capable CPU cores, an IPC proxy can reward speculative branch execution paths that fetch instructions without performing useful work, inflating measured IPC while degrading wall-clock latency, UPF IEEE 1801 power domain state preservation, and energy efficiency.

When we talk about proxy qualification, we must keep several relationships distinct. Numerical calibration gives us a declared mapping between our proxy outputs and much stronger reference outcomes. In contrast, confidence calibration asks whether our stated probabilities or confidence intervals actually match observed frequencies, a system-evaluation question we tackle fully in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect. To evaluate observed qualification coverage, we record our sampled dimensions, our specific test strata or cases, and the gaps between them. Ultimately, we must run separate tests to determine our held-out error, the stability of our candidate rankings, our estimation uncertainty, and the overall fitness of the proxy for our architecture decision.

In @fig-trust-calibration, we demonstrate that observed qualification cases and held-out agreement answer entirely separate questions by comparing conceptual normalized curves for a fast proxy metric against a heavy-weight reference tool across three distinct visual regions. On the left, green vertical bands highlight our sampled qualification strata, where paired proxy and reference observations directly anchor our confidence at discrete test points. Between the first two strata, a white dashed band marks an unsampled internal gap where no empirical qualification exists, demonstrating that smooth visual interpolation cannot guarantee proxy validity across unverified design points. Finally, as design search moves beyond our sampled support zone into the right-hand region, the curves diverge sharply, illustrating how an uncalibrated proxy score can completely part company from true physical performance. As a result, our schematic distinctly separates these observed strata from any internal gaps, as well as from extrapolation beyond our sampled design range.

![**Discrete qualification strata expose unsampled proxy evaluation gaps.** Our conceptual, normalized curves show paired proxy and stronger-reference observations in three sampled strata, an unsampled gap between them, and possible divergence as our search continues beyond those strata. In our real architectural studies, we must record the specific dimensions, sampled cases or strata, gaps, and held-out agreement. We emphasize that these curves are not measured data.](images/fig-trust-calibration){#fig-trust-calibration width="100%" fig-alt="Conceptual normalized plot with three separate green qualification strata in the left-hand range. Paired proxy and stronger-reference markers appear in each stratum, while a dashed white band marks an unsampled gap between the first two. The curves may diverge as search continues into an unqualified right-hand range. No plotted curve is measured data."}

An internal gap remains thoroughly unqualified even if both smooth curves happen to pass through it. We still need held-out comparisons to establish whether our estimation error and candidate ordering are actually adequate at the sampled strata. Whenever we move into that gap or venture beyond our observed range, we must perform new reference checks or provide a rigorous separate justification. The possible divergence on the right side of our plot serves as a stark, practical warning. We cannot automatically assume that a higher proxy score outside our qualified support zone translates to a stronger architecture result.

In our computer architecture community, techniques like SMARTS and SimPoint provide specific precedents for making robust population inferences. When we rigorously sample intervals from a declared benchmark execution stream, we can confidently support quantified performance estimates for that target execution population [@WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS; @SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint]. That powerful result does not automatically render an arbitrary held-out sample representative. When we conduct a new architecture study, we must explicitly declare our target population and rigorously justify our sampling design for it. Our inference simply does not extend to workloads, design candidates, EDA tools, or operating conditions outside the boundaries of those declarations.

We must recognize that numerical calibration and ranking fidelity answer fundamentally different questions. A numerically calibrated scalar mapping relates our proxy outputs to our heavy-weight reference outcomes under a strictly declared procedure, while a predictive interval explicitly adds a stated uncertainty model to our estimates [@ForresterSobesterKeane2008Surrogate]. On the other hand, ranking fidelity asks whether our candidate ordering actually survives the scrutiny of the stronger check. We can easily have low average error alongside entirely wrong orderings near a critical architectural decision boundary, just as we can have highly useful ordering alongside heavily biased absolute values. Proper qualification therefore reports the specific relationship our design decision requires, and it rigorously tests our proxy's error or instability against our explicitly declared margin.

Because a proxy can fail us in several distinct ways, and because each type of failure eliminates a different architectural inference, we must apply separate diagnostic tests for six primary concerns. In @tbl-proxy-diagnostics, we summarize these surrogate weaknesses alongside their required diagnostic checks and adverse inferences.

To systematically evaluate surrogate fitness, our diagnostic framework aligns each of the six concerns (Proxy mismatch, Observed qualification coverage, Held-out agreement, Confounding, Variability, and Selection bias) with a specific diagnostic check and an adverse inference. We evaluate proxy mismatch by comparing surrogate scores against heavy-weight signoff metrics on matched design cases, while coverage audits map discrete test strata to expose unsampled gaps. Held-out agreement checks ranking stability on unseen benchmark suites, and confounding tests hold EDA tool parameters fixed to isolate true hardware causality. Finally, variability tests measure dispersion across stochastic runs, while selection bias re-evaluates winning candidates on fresh seeds to strip away statistical luck.

| **Concern** | **Diagnostic check** | **What an adverse result means** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Proxy mismatch** | We compare the proxy with a more decision-relevant measurement on matched cases. | Our available evidence does not support carrying the proxy result to the stronger architectural claim. |
| **Observed qualification coverage** | We record the workload, candidate, tool, and condition dimensions. Place matched cases across sampled strata, and identify gaps our search may enter. | Our available evidence does not qualify a reported candidate outside sampled cases or inside an unqualified gap. |
| **Held-out agreement** | We measure error, ranking stability, and uncertainty against our decision margin on cases not used to fit or tune the proxy. | Our available evidence does not support reliable candidate ordering for the declared use, even at observed qualification cases. |
